name: Color System Discipline
summary: Constrain your palette to ~10 role-based values. Each additional color dilutes hierarchy and weakens the signal of what's interactive.
description: A disciplined color system uses a small, role-based palette rather than an ad-hoc collection of hex values. The working budget is roughly 10 distinct colors total: 1 primary brand color, 1 accent for emphasis and CTAs, 4–5 neutrals for text and surfaces, and 2–3 semantic colors (success, warning, error, optionally info). Tints and shades count as separate values — `#1a73e8` and `#1565c0` are two colors in your budget, not one. When palettes balloon past ~10 values, users lose the ability to distinguish what's interactive from what's decorative, and visual hierarchy collapses. Every new color must earn its place by representing a distinct role or state, not a one-off styling decision.
implications: Define every color by role (primary, accent, neutral-100…900, success, warning, error, surface) before assigning hex values
Cap total distinct color values at ~10 across the entire interface
Use a single neutral ramp of 4–5 steps for all grays — no near-duplicates like #333 and #2f2f2f
Reserve the accent color for the most important interactive elements; it loses meaning if applied broadly
Treat tints, shades, and gradient stops as part of the budget — count them
Codify the palette as design tokens so components reference roles, not raw hex
Add new colors only when introducing a new role or state, never for one-off component styling
violations: Page using 11+ distinct hex values where hierarchy between interactive and decorative elements becomes unclear
Multiple near-duplicate grays (e.g., #333, #2f2f2f, #2e2e2e) that add complexity without visual difference
Ad-hoc hex values dropped into individual components instead of referencing the system
Accent color used for both primary CTAs and decorative flourishes, diluting its call-to-action signal
Unbounded gradient stops introducing 4–5 new color values for a single hero section
No semantic colors defined — success and error states reuse brand colors, creating ambiguity
